title: Orphei mors
titleEn: The Death of Orpheus — Metamorphoses XI.1–84
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The women of the Cicones, dressed in animal skins and out of their senses, catch sight of Orpheus from a hilltop as he sets his songs to the strings, and throw a spear that is bound round with leaves and leaves a mark without a wound, and a stone that his music beats down in mid-air; but drums, pipes and shrieking drown the lyre out, and after that the weapons find him. They tear away the birds, snakes and beasts still spellbound by his voice, take up the tools of ploughmen who run from them, tear the oxen apart, and kill Orpheus himself; his head and his lyre go down the Hebrus still sounding, and come ashore on Lesbos, where Apollo turns to stone a snake that goes for the head. His shade finds Eurydice among the dutiful dead, and Bacchus fastens the women who watched into the ground, where they become oak.

sentences.t:
Carmine dum tali silvas animosque ferarum
Threicius vates et saxa sequentia ducit,
sentences.l: While with a song of that kind the Thracian bard draws the woods and the spirits of wild beasts and the rocks that follow him,
sentences.i: While the Thracian singer is drawing the woods after him with a song of that kind, and the hearts of wild animals, and the rocks that come behind,
sentences.n: Carmine ... tali, “with a song of that kind”, points back at a song already sung before this part opens. dum with the present indicative ducit is the ordinary “while” of a scene still in progress, and the present holds the reader inside it. One verb governs three objects — silvas, animos ferarum, saxa — so woods, hearts and stones are all being led by the same music. animos is “spirits, hearts”, not the beasts themselves. sequentia is a present participle used attributively: rocks that are following, not rocks that have followed. Threicius vates names Orpheus by his country and his office rather than by name, and vates is the singer as prophet and priest.

sentences.t:
ecce nurus Ciconum, tectae lymphata ferinis
pectora velleribus, tumuli de vertice cernunt
Orphea percussis sociantem carmina nervis.
sentences.l: look — the young wives of the Cicones, covered as to their frenzied breasts with the pelts of wild beasts, from the top of a mound catch sight of Orpheus matching his songs to the strings he has struck.
sentences.i: suddenly the Cicones' young women, their frenzied breasts covered with animal skins, see from the top of a rise Orpheus setting his songs to the strings he strikes.
sentences.n: tectae is a passive participle agreeing with nurus, and lymphata ... pectora is an accusative of the part affected — “covered as to their frenzied breasts”. This Greek accusative of respect after a passive participle is a standing feature of Latin verse, and it comes again at 47; English has to turn it into “their breasts covered”. lymphatus is to be out of one's mind, driven frantic. nurus is strictly a daughter-in-law and in verse any young married woman. ferinis velleribus, the pelts of wild animals, are the standing dress of Bacchus' women. ecce with the present cernunt drops the reader into the moment. In 5 sociare takes a dative, so percussis nervis is not an ablative absolute but the thing the song is being matched to.

sentences.t:
E quibus una, leves iactato crine per auras,
“en,” ait “en hic est nostri contemptor!”
sentences.l: One out of them, her hair flung through the light air, says, “See — see, here is the despiser of us!”
sentences.i: One of them, her hair thrown loose on the light air, cries: “There — there he is, the man who holds us in contempt!”
sentences.n: E quibus is partitive, “one out of them”. iactato crine is an ablative absolute with a prepositional phrase folded inside it, leves ... per auras: “her hair having been tossed through the light air”. en is the pointing interjection, “look”, and it is doubled. nostri is an objective genitive of nos, so contemptor nostri is “the despiser of us” — and the agent noun in -tor makes the contempt a standing office rather than a passing mood.

sentences.l: and she sent a spear at the singing mouth of Apollo's bard, which, bound over in front with leaves, made a mark without a wound;
sentences.i: and she let fly a spear at the singing mouth of Apollo's poet — but the point was bound round with leaves, and it left a mark and no wound;
sentences.n: in ora is an accusative of the goal, what she throws at, and ora is plural for a single mouth as regularly in verse. The adjective is the cruelty of the line: vocalia ora, the mouth that gives voice, is exactly what a weapon thrown at a singer is aimed at. vatis Apollinei is the bard belonging to Apollo, which is why Apollo comes back at 58. quae picks up hastam. praesuta is a rare compound of suo, to sew: the shaft was sewn over at the point with leaves — a thyrsus rather than a spear — and notam sine vulnere is the result.

sentences.t:
alterius telum lapis est, qui missus in ipso
aere concentu victus vocisque lyraeque est
ac veluti supplex pro tam furialibus ausis
ante pedes iacuit.
sentences.l: another woman's weapon is a stone, which, once thrown, was beaten in the air itself by the concord of voice and lyre, and lay before his feet like a suppliant in atonement for so frenzied an attempt.
sentences.i: another's weapon is a stone — but once thrown it was beaten in mid-air by the concord of voice and lyre, and lay at his feet like a suppliant begging pardon for so mad an attempt.
sentences.n: alterius is the genitive of alter, “of a second woman”. missus is the perfect passive participle of mitto, and in ipso / aere is split at the line-end from 10 to 11, so the stone hangs in the air for a whole line before the verb reaches it. concentu is the sounding-together of parts, and vocisque lyraeque with the doubled -que is the epic pairing. victus ... est is a perfect passive split apart by vocisque lyraeque, with the auxiliary pushed to the end of the line. ausis is the ablative plural of ausum, “a thing dared”, and pro here is “in atonement for”, so the stone takes up a suppliant's posture and asks pardon for the attempt. furialibus is Fury-like, and it prepares the Erinys named two lines later.

sentences.t:
Sed enim temeraria crescunt
bella modusque abiit, insanaque regnat Erinys.
sentences.l: But in fact reckless fighting grows and measure has gone, and the mad Fury reigns.
sentences.i: But the reckless fighting grows, all measure is gone, and the mad Fury is queen.
sentences.n: Sed enim is elliptical, “but the fact is”, and it turns the scene. temeraria ... bella is split across the line-end at 13–14 with crescunt shut between the adjective and its noun, so the fighting grows in the word order before it grows in the sense. modus is due measure, the limit a thing should keep, and abiit is a plain perfect, “has gone”. Erinys is a Greek Fury, singular here and treated as a ruling power: regnat is the verb of a monarch.

sentences.t:
Cunctaque tela forent cantu mollita, sed ingens
clamor et infracto Berecyntia tibia cornu
tympanaque et plausus et Bacchei ululatus
obstrepuere sono citharae:
sentences.l: And all the weapons would have been softened by his singing, but a huge shouting and the Berecyntian pipe with its bent horn and drums and hand-clapping and Bacchic howls drowned out the sound of the lyre:
sentences.i: And every weapon would have been softened by his song, had not a huge shouting, and the Berecyntian pipe with its bent horn, and drums and clapping and Bacchic screaming, drowned the sound of the lyre:
sentences.n: forent is an old form of essent, and cuncta tela forent mollita is an unreal apodosis — “all the weapons would have been softened” — with the sed clause standing in for the condition that cancels it. obstrepuere is the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere for obstrepuerunt, a form that recurs throughout this passage and will only be nudged at afterwards. obstrepo takes a dative of what it drowns, sono citharae. The Berecyntia tibia is the Phrygian pipe of Cybele, named from Mount Berecyntus, and infracto ... cornu is an ablative of description: its bell was bent up like a horn. tympana are hand-drums and ululatus the ritual howl — a whole rite's worth of noise set against one stringed instrument.

sentences.t:
tum denique saxa
non exauditi rubuerunt sanguine vatis.
sentences.l: then at last the stones went red with the blood of the bard who was not heard through.
sentences.i: then at last the stones went red with the blood of the poet, no longer heard.
sentences.n: exaudio is to catch a sound clearly, to hear a thing through to the end. non exauditi ... vatis is a genitive going with sanguine, wrapped around the verb, and it gives the reason the stones now find their mark: his voice no longer reaches them. tum denique, “then and only then”, is the hinge of the episode — the music, and nothing else, had been what turned the weapons aside. rubuerunt is inceptive in force: they went red.

sentences.t:
Ac primum attonitas etiamnum voce canentis
innumeras volucres anguesque agmenque ferarum
Maenades, Orphei titulum, rapuere, theatri.
sentences.l: And first the countless birds, still at that moment thunderstruck by the voice of him singing, and the snakes and the column of wild beasts, the Maenads tore away — the boast of Orpheus' theatre.
sentences.i: And first the Maenads tore away the countless birds still spellbound by the singer's voice, and the snakes, and the massed ranks of beasts — the pride of Orpheus' audience.
sentences.n: attonitas, “thunderstruck”, agrees with volucres and stands four words in front of it. canentis is a participle used as a noun, “of him singing”. agmen is the word for a column on the march, and it will be used of the women themselves at 34. Orphei ... theatri titulum is in apposition to the whole list of creatures: a titulus is an inscription, and so a title of honour, a claim to fame. Both genitives belong to it — Orphei theatri, “of Orpheus' theatre” — so the creatures were the boast of his auditorium. The apposition is split by the verb, and theatri, the genitive that completes it, is held back to the last word of the line. Magnus prints theatri, the assembled audience; some editions print triumphi, “of his triumph”. rapuere is the same -ere perfect as at 18.

sentences.t:
Inde cruentatis vertuntur in Orphea dextris
et coeunt ut aves, si quando luce vagantem
noctis avem cernunt.
sentences.l: Then with bloodied right hands they turn on Orpheus, and they come together as birds do, if ever they catch sight of the bird of night straying in daylight.
sentences.i: Then, their hands already bloody, they round on Orpheus, and gather as birds do when they catch the night-bird abroad in daylight.
sentences.n: cruentatis ... dextris is an ablative absolute doing the work of a description: their right hands already bloodied. vertuntur in is passive in form with middle sense — they turn themselves — and in with the accusative is the hostile “against”. The simile is introduced by ut with si quando, “if ever”, the generalising conditional English says with “whenever”. noctis avem is the owl, and vagantem agrees with it across the line-end from 24 to 25, so the bird is seen straying before it is named. Small birds mobbing an owl caught out in daylight is the observed fact behind the comparison, and its point is the number and the daylight, not courage.

sentences.t:
Structoque utrimque theatro
ceu matutina cervus periturus harena
praeda canum est,
sentences.l: And, with the theatre built up on both sides, just as a stag that is going to die on the morning sand is the prey of the dogs,
sentences.i: And as, in an amphitheatre banked on both sides, a stag that will die on the morning sand is the dogs' prey,
sentences.n: structo ... theatro is an ablative absolute: the tiers raised on either side. The comparison is Roman and contemporary rather than heroic — matutina harena is the morning's sand, when the beast-hunts were staged, before the day's other killings. periturus is a future participle, “about to die”, and Latin uses it of what is already settled rather than merely expected. theatrum was used at 22 of the crowd Orpheus drew; the same word now means the stands an animal is killed in front of.

sentences.t:
vatemque petunt et fronde virentes
coniciunt thyrsos non haec in munera factos.
sentences.l: so they make for the bard and hurl thyrsi green with foliage, made not for these duties.
sentences.i: so they come at the poet, and fling the thyrsi, green with leaves, that were never made for work of this kind.
sentences.n: petunt is “make for, go at”, the ordinary verb of an attack. fronde virentes is an ablative of respect with the participle, “green with foliage”. A thyrsus is the Bacchic wand — a fennel stalk wound with ivy and tipped with a pine-cone, a ritual object and not a weapon, which is what non haec in munera factos says: in with the accusative is “for” of purpose, and munera are the duties a thing is made for. But munus is also the technical Latin word for a public spectacle of exactly the kind the simile has just described, so the phrase can be read twice over.

sentences.t:
Hae glaebas, illae direptos arbore ramos,
pars torquent silices.
sentences.l: These hurl clods of earth, those branches torn from a tree, a part flints.
sentences.i: Some throw clods of earth, some branches torn off a tree, some flints.
sentences.n: One verb, torquent, serves three subjects and three objects and is held back to the second line. hae ... illae ... pars is “these ... those ... a part”, and pars is a collective singular taking a plural verb, which Latin allows freely. direptos arbore is an ablative of separation with no preposition, “torn from a tree”. torqueo is to whirl a thing before letting it go, the proper verb for a sling or a hurled stone, and it will come back at 70 as the twisting of a root.

sentences.t:
Neu desint tela furori,
forte boves presso subigebant vomere terram,
sentences.l: And so that weapons should not be lacking to their frenzy, as it happened oxen were breaking up the earth with the ploughshare pressed down,
sentences.i: And — so that their frenzy should not run short of weapons — as it happened, oxen were working the soil with the share pressed deep,
sentences.n: neu is neve, “and that ... not”, a negative purpose clause, and desum takes a dative, furori. The subjunctive is present although the surrounding narrative is past, which keeps the clause vivid; the joke is in the construction itself, since the sentence arranges the countryside as though the scene had a purpose. forte, “as it happened”, then does the opposite and calls it chance. subigere terram is the standard phrase for turning soil, and presso vomere is the ablative of the share bearing down.

sentences.t:
nec procul hinc multo fructum sudore parantes
dura lacertosi fodiebant arva coloni.
sentences.l: and not far from here, getting their crop with much sweat, brawny farmers were digging the hard fields.
sentences.i: and not far off, earning their crop with a great deal of sweat, sinewy farmhands were breaking the hard ground.
sentences.n: multo ... sudore wraps around fructum, so the sweat encloses the crop. parantes agrees with coloni, which is held to the very last word of 33 behind its own adjective and its verb: dura lacertosi fodiebant arva coloni interlocks two noun-and-adjective pairs, dura ... arva and lacertosi ... coloni. lacertosus is from lacertus, the upper arm — muscular, thick in the arm. The imperfects here and at 31 set an ordinary working morning going in the background.

sentences.t:
Agmine qui viso fugiunt operisque relinquunt
arma sui,
sentences.l: And they, when the column had been seen, flee and leave behind the weapons of their own work,
sentences.i: And they, seeing the column come on, run for it and leave behind the weapons of their trade,
sentences.n: qui is a connecting relative opening the sentence — “and they”, the farmers — which English turns into an ordinary pronoun. agmine viso is an ablative absolute, and agmen is the same military word used of the beasts at 21: the audience and the mob get the same noun. arma operis sui is the sting, since arma are weapons of war, and the phrase calls hoes and rakes “the weapons of their work” one line before they become weapons in fact. operis and sui are split across the line-end from 34 to 35.

sentences.t:
vacuosque iacent dispersa per agros
sarculaque rastrique graves longique ligones.
sentences.l: and scattered through the empty fields there lie hoes and heavy rakes and long mattocks.
sentences.i: and hoes and heavy rakes and long mattocks lie scattered over the emptied fields.
sentences.n: dispersa is a neuter plural participle whose nouns do not arrive until the whole of 36, so the reader is told that things are lying scattered before being told what they are. vacuos ... per agros wraps around the verb, and the fields are empty because the previous sentence has just emptied them. The three tools are strung on -que ... -que ... -que, a piling-up where English would want commas. A ligo is a broad-bladed mattock and a rastrum a heavy toothed drag; both are named here by weight and length, which is what makes them serve.

sentences.t:
Quae postquam rapuere ferae cornuque minaci
divulsere boves,
sentences.l: And after the wild women had snatched these up and, for all the menacing horn, torn the oxen apart,
sentences.i: And when the savage women had caught these up and torn the oxen apart, menacing horns and all,
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative, “and these”, the tools. ferae is the adjective “wild” standing on its own as the noun for the women, so a word used of the animals all through this passage is turned on them. rapuere and divulsere are both -ere perfects. Magnus prints cornu minaci, the ablative agreeing with cornu: the menace belongs to the ox's own horn, and the ablative is best taken as attendant circumstance — the women tore the animals apart in spite of it — though it can also be read as an ablative of means, the horns taken hold of and used. Some editions print minaces, nominative, which makes the women the threatening ones instead.

sentences.t:
ad vatis fata recurrunt
Tendentemque manus et in illo tempore primum
inrita dicentem nec quicquam voce moventem
sacrilegae perimunt.
sentences.l: they run back to the bard's death; and him, stretching out his hands and at that moment for the first time saying things that had no effect and moving nothing with his voice, the sacrilegious women destroy.
sentences.i: they run back to finish the poet; and as he stretches out his hands and for the first time speaks to no effect, moving nothing at all with his voice, those sacrilegious women kill him.
sentences.n: fata, “the fates”, is the ordinary poetic plural for a death. Orpheus is present in this sentence only as three accusative participles — tendentem, dicentem, moventem — with no noun or pronoun for them to agree with, so English has to supply the “him” the Latin withholds. inrita is a neuter plural adjective standing as the object of dicentem, “saying ineffectual things”, and nec quicquam moventem is the same shape over again with an indefinite pronoun. sacrilegae, one adjective, is the whole subject, “the sacrilegious women”, and the charge is exact, since he is Apollo's own bard. The edition prints Tendentemque with a capital at the start of 39 although no sentence begins there — the sentence started at 37 and runs on to perimunt in 41. Every other line in this part that opens with a capital either begins a sentence or begins with a proper name or an adjective made from one. The capital is the edition's and is kept as archived; nothing is claimed about what the second witness prints.

sentences.t:
Perque os, pro Iuppiter! illud
auditum saxis intellectumque ferarum
sensibus in ventos anima exhalata recessit.
sentences.l: And through that mouth — great Jupiter! — heard by rocks and understood by the senses of wild beasts, his breath, breathed out, withdrew into the winds.
sentences.i: And through that mouth — Jupiter! — that rocks had heard and the senses of wild beasts had understood, his life was breathed out and went away into the winds.
sentences.n: pro here is not the preposition but the interjection of outcry, taking a vocative: pro Iuppiter is “great Jupiter!”, the narrator breaking in on his own sentence. Per ... os ... illud is split around that outcry and then held open across the line-end so that the two participles in 42 can be hung on it. auditum saxis and intellectum ferarum sensibus have datives of the agent, a use verse allows freely with a perfect passive participle. anima is breath and life in one word, and exhalata makes the double sense literal: the last breath out of that mouth is the soul. recessit, “withdrew”, is the only finite verb in the sentence, and it is a quiet one.

sentences.t:
Te maestae volucres, Orpheu, te turba ferarum,
te rigidi silices, tua carmina saepe secutae
fleverunt silvae, positis te frondibus arbor
tonsa comas luxit.
sentences.l: You the mourning birds, Orpheus, you the throng of wild beasts, you the unyielding flints, and the woods that had often followed your songs, wept for; and with its leaves laid down the tree, shorn as to its hair, mourned you.
sentences.i: You the birds mourned, Orpheus, you the throng of beasts, you the unyielding flints, and the woods that had followed your songs so often; and the tree let its leaves fall and, its hair cut short, grieved for you.
sentences.n: Apostrophe: the poem turns out of the narrative to address Orpheus. te stands four times, but the four are not alike: three of them (twice in 44, once in 45) are the object of fleverunt, which does not arrive until 46, and the fourth, in 46 itself, belongs to luxit at the start of 47. The fourth subject of fleverunt, silvae, carries no te of its own, so the run of address is three, not four. Orpheu is a Greek vocative. secutae agrees with silvae and is separated from it by the line-end. Magnus prints tua carmina; some editions print te carmina, which would put a fourth te into the fleverunt series. positis frondibus is an ablative absolute, the leaves laid down, and tonsa comas is another Greek accusative of respect, “shorn as to her hair”, of the kind first met at 3: the tree's foliage is her hair, and cutting the hair is a mourner's act, so the tree performs a human funeral.

sentences.t:
Lacrimis quoque flumina dicunt
increvisse suis,
sentences.l: They say too that the rivers rose with tears of their own,
sentences.i: They say that the rivers too rose with weeping of their own,
sentences.n: dicunt is the indefinite third person plural with no subject expressed, “they say”, and it introduces an indirect statement: flumina is the accusative subject and increvisse the perfect infinitive. suis agrees with lacrimis and is held to the far side of the infinitive, so the ablative phrase wraps the whole clause — which is the point, since the rivers rose with tears of their own and not with rain. quoque here is the adverb “too”, not the relative quo with -que attached; the same string of letters can be either, and it is worth checking every time.

sentences.t:
obstrusaque carbasa pullo
naides et dryades passosque habuere capillos.
sentences.l: and the naiads and dryads had their linen overlaid with mourning black and their hair let loose.
sentences.i: and naiads and dryads wore linen darkened with mourning black, and their hair unbound.
sentences.n: habuere is habuerunt again, and it governs two objects each carrying a participle — carbasa obstrusa and capillos passos — in the idiom “to have a thing in a state”, that is, to wear it so. obstrudo is to thrust one thing over another, so the mourning colour is thought of as pushed over the white linen; the word is a hard one and the sense is “overlaid, muffled”. pullum is the dark undyed wool the Romans wore in mourning, and carbasa is a fine linen. passos is from pando, to spread out, not from patior: loosened hair, the other Roman sign of grief. Both signs are transferred here to water- and tree-nymphs.

sentences.t: Membra iacent diversa locis.
sentences.l: The limbs lie sundered, in separate places.
sentences.i: His limbs lie scattered, each in a different place.
sentences.n: Four words, and the shortest sentence in the part: the killing itself was given a single verb at 41, and the scattered body is given these four words. diversa is predicative with iacent — they lie sundered — and locis is a bare ablative of place where, without a preposition, which verse allows. membra carries no possessive at all: the Latin does not say whose limbs they are.

sentences.t:
Caput, Hebre, lyramque
excipis,
sentences.l: The head, Hebrus, and the lyre you take up;
sentences.i: The head, Hebrus, and the lyre — you catch them up;
sentences.n: Apostrophe again, and this time to a river: Hebre is a vocative and excipis a second person, so the poem stops to speak to the Thracian Hebrus itself. excipio is the verb for catching a thing as it falls, or receiving what is carried down to you. The two objects, caput and lyram, will govern a feminine plural participle at 54.

sentences.t:
et (mirum!) medio dum labitur amne,
flebile nescio quid queritur lyra, flebile lingua
murmurat exanimis, respondent flebile ripae.
sentences.l: and — a wonder! — while it glides down mid-stream, the lyre complains something mournful, the lifeless tongue murmurs something mournful, and mournfully the banks answer.
sentences.i: and — a wonder — as it drifts down midstream the lyre makes some mournful complaint, the dead tongue murmurs something mournful, and mournfully the banks answer back.
sentences.n: nescio quid is a fixed indefinite, “something or other”, with nescio worn down into part of the phrase rather than a real “I do not know”. flebile stands three times: first as the adjective of nescio quid; then on its own with murmurat, where it can be read either as an object, “something mournful”, or adverbially; and last plainly adverbially with respondent, “mournfully”. medio ... amne is an ablative of place split around dum labitur. exanimis agrees with lingua but is held over the line-end from 52 to 53, so the tongue is heard murmuring before the reader is told that it is dead. respondent is the ordinary verb of an echo, and the banks answer with the very word they are answering.

sentences.t:
Iamque mare invectae flumen populare relinquunt
et Methymnaeae potiuntur litore Lesbi.
sentences.l: And now, borne out into the sea, they leave the river of their own people and gain the shore of Methymnaean Lesbos.
sentences.i: And now, carried out to sea, they leave their own country's river behind and reach the shore of Methymnaean Lesbos.
sentences.n: invectae is a feminine plural participle although what is being carried down is a head, which is neuter, and a lyre, which is feminine: the participle follows the feminine of the pair, and there is no clean grammatical antecedent for it. mare is a bare accusative of the goal of motion with the participle, a Greek construction Latin verse borrows. populare is from populus, “of the people” — the river of his own country, not “popular”. potior is deponent and takes an ablative, litore. Methymna is a city of Lesbos, and Lesbi is a Greek genitive; the island is the home of Greek lyric poetry, so the head that is still singing comes ashore in a fitting place.

sentences.t:
Hic ferus expositum peregrinis anguis harenis
os petit et sparsos stillanti rore capillos.
sentences.l: Here a savage snake makes for the head laid out on the foreign sand, and the hair sprinkled with dripping moisture.
sentences.i: Here a savage snake goes for the head as it lies on that foreign sand, and for the hair still dripping with the sea.
sentences.n: The word order weaves two pairs through each other: ferus ... anguis is interrupted by expositum peregrinis, and expositum ... os is the pair split at the line-end, reaching its noun only at the start of 57. petit is “makes for”, the ordinary verb of an attack. peregrinis harenis is an ablative of place, and peregrinus is the word for a foreigner, so the sand is foreign to what has washed up on it. ros is properly dew, and in verse any liquid falling in drops; here it is the sea still running out of the hair.

sentences.t:
Tandem Phoebus adest morsusque inferre parantem
arcet et in lapidem rictus serpentis apertos
congelat et patulos, ut erant, indurat hiatus.
sentences.l: At last Phoebus is there and wards it off as it makes ready to bring its bite to bear, and freezes the serpent's open jaws into stone and hardens the wide gape, just as they were.
sentences.i: At last Phoebus is there: he stops the snake as it makes ready to strike, freezes its open jaws to stone, and hardens them wide open, just as they were.
sentences.n: Tandem, “at last”, answers Apollinei at 8: the god whose bard he was arrives now. parantem is accusative agreeing with the snake, with no pronoun expressed, and morsus inferre is the standing idiom for bringing a bite to bear. in lapidem with congelat is the accusative of the thing something is turned into. ut erant is a two-word parenthesis and it is the whole point of the change: the jaws are fixed at the instant of the strike and stay open. rictus and hiatus are both plural for one mouth, as verse regularly is with parts of the body, and erant is plural with them: “just as they were”, not “as it was”.

sentences.t:
Umbra subit terras et quae loca viderat ante,
cuncta recognoscit quaerensque per arva piorum
invenit Eurydicen cupidisque amplectitur ulnis.
sentences.l: His shade goes down beneath the earth, and the places it had seen before, all of them, it knows again, and searching through the fields of the dutiful it finds Eurydice and embraces her with longing arms.
sentences.i: His shade goes down under the earth and knows again every place it had seen before; and searching the fields of the blessed, he finds Eurydice and takes her in his arms with all his longing.
sentences.n: quae loca viderat ante, cuncta puts the relative clause in front of its own antecedent and then gathers it up with cuncta — “all the places, whichever he had seen before”. Latin does this freely and English cannot follow. umbra, the shade, is the subject of all four verbs. arva piorum is the part of the underworld kept for the dutiful. Eurydicen is a Greek accusative. ulnae are the forearms, so the noun makes the embrace physical, and cupidis supplies the wanting.

sentences.t: Hic modo coniunctis spatiantur passibus ambo,
sentences.l: Here at one moment the two of them walk about with steps joined together,
sentences.i: Here at one moment the two of them stroll side by side, in step,
sentences.n: modo here is “at one moment”, answered by nunc ... nunc in the next line: a three-part alternation, not a sequence of events. spatiantur is deponent and means to walk about at leisure — the verb of a stroll, not of a journey. coniunctis passibus is an ablative of manner, their steps joined. ambo is the word Latin keeps for two taken together, as against duo for two counted.

sentences.t:
nunc praecedentem sequitur, nunc praevius anteit
Eurydicenque suam iam tutus respicit Orpheus.
sentences.l: now he follows her going in front, now, leading, he goes ahead, and Orpheus, safe now, looks back at his own Eurydice.
sentences.i: now he follows her as she goes ahead, now he takes the lead and walks in front — and Orpheus, safe now, looks back at his Eurydice.
sentences.n: praecedentem is a bare accusative feminine participle: Eurydice, unnamed until the next line. praevius is a predicate adjective where English wants an adverb, “going in front”. anteit scans as two syllables here, the e and the i run together by synizesis. The line goes nunc prae- / ce-den- / tem se-qui- / tur nunc / prae-vi-us / an-teit: the fifth foot is the dactyl prae-vi-us, with the final -us light before the opening vowel of anteit, and the sixth is the spondee an-teit. Read anteit as three syllables and the line has a foot too many. respicit is the exact verb for looking back, and iam tutus, “safe now”, is where the line rests. Magnus prints tutus, the adjective, making the safety his condition; some editions print tuto, the adverb, making it the manner of the look.

sentences.t: Non impune tamen scelus hoc sinit esse Lyaeus,
sentences.l: Yet Lyaeus does not allow this crime to be unpunished,
sentences.i: But Lyaeus does not let the crime go unpunished:
sentences.n: impune is an adverb, so sinit hoc scelus esse impune is “allows this crime to be without-penalty”, with no adjective in the Latin at all. tamen sets the sentence against everything that has happened since 41. Lyaeus is a cult title of Bacchus, the Greek Lyaios, “the Loosener”, from the verb to untie — and it is the name chosen for a god who is about to tie the guilty down.

sentences.t:
amissoque dolens sacrorum vate suorum
protinus in silvis matres Edonidas omnes,
quae videre nefas, torta radice ligavit.
sentences.l: and grieving that the bard of his own rites had been lost, at once, in the woods, he bound all the Edonian mothers who had seen the abomination with a twisted root.
sentences.i: and grieving for the lost poet of his own rites, he fastened down on the spot, in the woods, every Edonian woman who had watched the sacrilege, with a twisted root.
sentences.n: amisso ... vate is an ablative absolute doing the work of a causal clause with dolens: “with the bard lost”. sacrorum suorum is a genitive — Orpheus is Bacchus' own priest, which is what makes the killing sacrilege as well as murder. Edonidas is a Greek accusative plural, the women of the Edoni, a people of Thrace, and matres is simply grown women. videre in 70 is the poetic third-plural perfect for viderunt, “they saw”, not the infinitive; the two forms are spelt alike and only the sense settles it. nefas is what divine law forbids. torta radice is an ablative of means, and torqueo is the verb the women themselves were given at 30 for hurling flints.

sentences.t:
Quippe pedum digitos, in quantum est quaeque secuta,
traxit et in solidam detrusit acumina terram,
sentences.l: Yes — the toes of their feet, to the extent that each had followed, he drew out, and drove their points down into the solid earth,
sentences.i: For he drew out the toes of their feet — each in proportion to how far she had joined the chase — and drove the points down into the hard ground,
sentences.n: Quippe introduces the explanation of ligavit: the way of it was this. pedum digitos are the toes. in quantum est quaeque secuta is “to the extent that each had pursued”, with the perfect deponent secuta est split apart by quaeque, so each woman's root goes down in proportion to her own share of the chase and the punishment is measured out individually. acumina are the points — the toes now drawn to a tip and treated as root-ends. Magnus prints in quantum; the second witness reads via quam tum, which will not construe as it stands and looks like a corruption of the same phrase.

sentences.t:
utque suum laqueis, quos callidus abdidit auceps,
crus ubi commisit volucris sensitque teneri,
plangitur ac trepidans adstringit vincula motu:
sentences.l: and just as, when a bird has committed its own leg to the snares that a cunning fowler has hidden, and has felt itself held, it beats itself and, panicking, pulls the bonds tight by its own movement:
sentences.i: and just as, when a bird has put its leg into the snare a cunning fowler has hidden and feels itself held, it beats its wings and, panicking, draws the noose tighter by its own struggling:
sentences.n: suum and crus are split across the line-end from 73 to 74 with a whole relative clause between them, so the word order tangles the bird's leg before the sense does. committere takes a dative, laqueis: to entrust a limb to the snare. sensit teneri is an indirect statement with a passive infinitive and no expressed subject — it felt itself to be held. plangitur is passive in form with middle force, “beats itself”, not “is beaten”, and the same verb returns at 81 of a woman beating her thigh. adstringit vincula motu is the cruelty of the simile: the struggling is exactly what tightens the bonds. The edition's ad- spelling in adstringit is its own and is kept.

sentences.t:
sic, ut quaeque solo defixa cohaeserat harum,
exsternata fugam frustra temptabat;
sentences.l: so, just as each of these women had stuck fast, fixed in the ground, driven out of her senses she kept trying flight in vain;
sentences.i: so each of them, driven out of her senses, held fast where she had been fixed in the ground, kept trying to run and could not;
sentences.n: sic answers the utque of 73 and closes the simile. ut quaeque ... cohaeserat is “just as each of them had”, with harum, a partitive genitive, held to the end of the line behind its own verb. defixa is driven down and fixed in place, the word used of a stake. exsternata is to be driven out of one's senses by fear; the edition's exs- spelling is its own. temptabat is imperfect — the attempt goes on and does not stop, which is what frustra is measuring.

sentences.t:
at illam
lenta tenet radix exsultantemque coercet,
sentences.l: but the pliant root holds her and pens her in as she plunges,
sentences.i: but the tough root holds her fast and reins her in as she throws herself about,
sentences.n: lenta is the adjective for wood that is tough and pliant at once — it bends and does not break — and both halves of the sense are wanted, since the root gives and still holds. illam ... exsultantem is a single accusative with the verbs set inside it: illam is the object of tenet, and exsultantem agrees with it as the object of coercet. exsulto is the frequentative of exsilio, to keep leaping up, and it is used of an animal that will not be held. coerceo is the word for penning stock in.

sentences.t:
dumque ubi sint digiti, dum pes ubi, quaerit, et ungues,
adspicit in teretes lignum succedere suras,
sentences.l: and while she asks where her toes are, where her foot is, and her nails, she sees wood coming up over her smooth calves,
sentences.i: and while she is asking where her toes are, and where her foot, and her nails, she sees the wood climbing over her smooth calves,
sentences.n: Two indirect questions with ubi and the subjunctive sint, both governed by quaerit — which is held back until after them, and then et ungues is tacked on outside its own clause, so the question comes apart as she asks it. The second question has no verb at all: dum pes ubi. teres is the adjective for a shape turned smooth on a lathe. adspicit governs an accusative and infinitive, lignum succedere, so the wood is the subject of the infinitive and not the object of the verb: she sees that wood is coming up over her calves.

sentences.t:
et conata femur maerenti plangere dextra,
robora percussit:
sentences.l: and having tried to beat her thigh with a grieving right hand, she struck oak:
sentences.i: and trying to beat her thigh with a mourning hand, she struck hard oak:
sentences.n: conata is the perfect participle of the deponent conor, so it is active in sense — “having tried” — although its ending is a passive one. Beating the thigh with the flat of the hand is the Roman gesture of grief, and plangere is the same verb the caught bird was given at 75. maerenti belongs by sense to the woman and is handed to her hand instead, a transferred epithet. robur is oak, and hard wood in general; the plural is used of a mass of it.

sentences.t:
pectus quoque robora fiunt,
robora sunt umeri, porrectaque bracchia veros
esse putes ramos, et non fallere putando.
sentences.l: her breast too becomes oak, oak are her shoulders, and the arms stretched out you would suppose to be real branches — and that you are not going wrong in supposing it.
sentences.i: her breast too turns to oak, her shoulders are oak, and you would take the outstretched arms for real branches — and taking them so, you would not be wrong.
sentences.n: fiunt is plural although its subject pectus is singular: the verb has been drawn into the number of its predicate, robora. robora then stands three times in two lines, and the repetition is the change itself. putes is a potential subjunctive with the indefinite second person, “one would think”. The last clause keeps the same verb: et non fallere putando is still governed by putes, so it is “and would think that one is not going wrong in thinking it”, with putando an ablative gerund of means. Magnus prints porrecta bracchia, arms stretched out; some editions read nodosa, “knotted”, which makes them already gnarled. Magnus prints fallere, the active infinitive still hanging on putes; some editions print fallare, the second-person passive subjunctive, which takes the clause out of putes and lets it stand on its own: “and you would not be deceived in thinking so”.
